I have no right to write to you. I left you behind, after all.
But now, I believe I must write this letter to you.
You asked me once: what can I do to get through these torturous days?
To put it another way, am I prepared to kill someone, even an enemy of mine?
Back then, I could not give you an answer. But now, I think I might have something to say.
Before I made my move, someone told me my sentence could be shortened, or I could even avoid serving jail time entirely had I wanted. A new life would await me once I got my fortune and my property back.
When I heard this proposal, I felt fear.
In Mansfield Prison, I met all sorts of inmates. They were in there for all kinds of different reasons, but personally, I doubt many are innately evil. Most of them were just people who could not endure their pain and had finally succumbed to fate. After coming to Rhodes Island, I have stood shoulder to shoulder with many fighters as they faced Oripathy and challenged their unfair fates. They are extremely brave, yet they pay a heavy price.
There are many who lack the power or means to overcome the hardships in their way, and many more who struggle to wage war against their own fates, so much so that I felt a sort of guilt when I realized I had the ability to control my own, and to embrace what you could call a happy life.
I know this too is but a kind of arrogance, and no one will be grateful for my guilt. Even if I don't lend a hand, no one will comment on my lack of action—after all, everyone is simply facing their own difficulties with all they have.
But since I do feel guilt, since I do have the ability to overcome my hardships, rather than carry on a perpetual confession of my crime, I believe I should bear it on my back, displaying it to everyone out there. To show those trying to run from their own fates what it's like to face your own destiny, and to help strengthen the resolve of those about to lose their courage to do so.
So I rejected that proposal, and once I was done with my revenge, I turned myself in.
At my parents' funeral, I said I was free. That was no lie. To me, being in prison does not mean losing my freedom. I exacted my vengeance, my anger has been quelled, and my hatred is finally gone.
I chose to face my own fate, so I should shoulder my sins as I deserve.
Speaking of which, I will be incarcerated in Mansfield again. It seems I really do have a connection to that place.
I will go back, and this time I'll have a chat with the prisoners to see what more I can do for them. When my sentence is over, I think I will return to Rhodes Island, or perhaps do the sort of work Rhodes Island would. Who knows?
I say all this... in the hopes that it will reassure you that I have not been crushed or paralyzed by the weight of my sins.
I only chose an arduous path for myself. But please believe me when I say that no matter how long it takes, we will meet again at the end of this road.

He opens his eyes, flickering silently in the depths of incense billowing from the censer. He feels—
Shattered.
The pain bites at his consciousness, charging straight at its source, and it seems that this wisp of smoke, this tiny flame is his body. No, he remembers that he had once been able to analyze all things in this world, level mountains and lay waste to cities with a flick of his tail. However, his consciousness should not have arisen from the midst of this chaos, for that which slumbers yet sleeps, and naught has changed since. The tendrils of smoke weave their way through the netting, sinking down to the base of the censer, where the wispy cloud swallows him whole. Why do I awaken? Why do I struggle? Why is it that at the deepest part of this tomb-like jail, there is an even narrower cage? His eyes become smoke, and he gorges himself on his own body, letting off a roar of fury at the nothingness before him.
The smoke shifts imperceptibly, as if a minute breeze has swept across the chamber of stone. He remembers—
Humiliation.
A great hunt, his defeat, the shame engraved on his bones and inscribed on his heart. His fury draws a picture of the past, where the strong were brought low by the weak, ancient time was overwritten by fleeting moment, and gods were toppled by commoners. The True Lung bled before the people, boiling copper and molten gold pouring onto the earth. For three thousand days and nights, smiths chiseled deep ravines into mountains, casting myriad forms of weapons. The altar became a stronghold, and the robes of the devotees burning incense concealed blades of edict divine. Yes, this was the price of such trickery. An incisive punitive strike, a wound that could not heal. The traces of this humiliation still reside in his body, and he plans to use this wound as a mold to cast a sword.
A flame bursts forth from the censer as if pumped by a bellows, and the Candleholder on guard rings the alarm bell. He raises—
A blade.
Within the boundless gloom, there are still other consciousnesses being born. At the moment, those consciousnesses are not as lucid as he, but they are as he, and they too seek to surface from the depths of this turbid pond. He still remembers how mortals would describe this sort of relationship, and he understands that they will be his... brothers and sisters. He endures the pain, as though his stomach had been split in twain, and flicks his wrist. The cloud of smoke bursts and dissipates, his sword rending apart heaven and earth from within the chaos.
The primordial fog shrinks back, and gloomy night becomes brightest day.
The Candleholders rush into the stone chamber, and the Imperial Guards surround the tomb layer by layer. At last, he feels—
Freedom.
The smoke rises from the censer in spirals, standing steady on its stone platform. In the depths of its belly, the Feranmut yet slumbers. He feels that his own body has become lighter, as if he has turned into a wisp of smoke rising through a hole in the censer, floating across the heads of the Candleholders and Imperial Guards, floating past the sealed stone door of the mausoleum, floating through the skies above Baizao, towards distant lands.

Punch, relax, inhale, exhale—breathing out impurities. The breath leaves him like a lingering fog, spiraling through the air for some time. The sky has just cleared after a rain, and the slippery puddles reflect the grandmaster as he practices.
Mirrored movements at mirrored speeds, yet a thread of disharmony can be seen in this mirror image.
Chongyue halts and looks around.
The breath slowly forms into a shape with a head and tail—the shadow of a beast. It clings to his feet, eyes glaring like daggers.
Mobilizing his Qi, the grandmaster shifts position and surges forward with a flip. Clouds move and light shifts. The shadow twists, using the surrounding shadows to form a beast tail that threatens to strike him down.
He dodges and thrusts his palm, dispersing the tail instantly. But by then, the white fog has grown large. It opens its maw and bares its claws, poised to attack.
'Hah!'
With a cry that shakes the earth, he tightens his fist, gathers force, and unleashes a punch. Wind whips as it connects, scattering the fog, yet it condenses again into a larger and now grayish-black beast, darkening the sun with its form. It narrows its eyes at the 'human' before it.
'I know you won't give up that easily. Come; be it a hundred or a thousand times, I won't back down.'
The enraged beast stirs a wild gale, leaves sticking to it like green scales. It opens its jaws wide and charges at Chongyue.
He makes no move to avoid it, taking the full brunt of its fearsome blow. With a push of his palm, he sends it reeling.
'What words can't convey, my actions will.'
He dashes forth, palm now again a fist, and slams down with all his might.
A dull thud resounds across heaven and earth, followed by a violent roar.
He does not stop, instead raining down blow after blow, until the beast can no longer lift its head. Thunder rolls and dark clouds gather, but the beast seems to show slight signs of surrender.
'A usual sparring would end here, but between us, I must go all out. Apologies!'
Chongyue leaps into the air, his body light as a feather, his fist heavy as a mountain. With a single strike, he punches a hole straight through his foe.
With this upper hand, he presses the attack. His fists become palms, then claws—his left tears as his right clutches—and the beast roars, unwilling to admit defeat. But in the end, the fog disperses, bereft of form and spirit. After a while, the sun begins to shine once more. Where the bestial shadow once swept, a sword now remains.

Demetri thought his words were naive. Not that there was anything wrong with naivete, of course. It was only natural that the future Don should expand his horizons, so that when the time came to take over, he would have the vision to see the big picture and choose the best course of action. He would have to understand and take care of all of the famiglia's members, and ensure Bellone's continued prosperity. Though Leon's path had deviated somewhat from his expectations, Demetri had believed that he would groom Leon into the perfect Don, at which point he and his knife would become the Don's perfect tools.
Thinking back now, perhaps he was the truly naive one.
Demetri cuts the ice cube into a sphere with his knife, and places it into the glass. This knife has been with him for so many years and remains a useful instrument to this day; he is much the same.
uniequip_002_svrash:
When it awoke, it found itself lying in a warm room.
The unfamiliar environment frightened it and it wanted to leave, but it was in so much pain it could not move.
The door opened, and through it strode a Feline boy with silver hair and a thick tail. He approached it with liniment and gauze in hand, applying the medicine in the bottle to the wound before bandaging it up.
It struggled a little at first, but was too weak to do anything but accept the boy's treatment before falling into a deep slumber.
On the second day, the boy took it back to where it had been found. They wandered through the woods for an entire day until the boy was exhausted and gasping for breath, but in the end found only the remains of two adult fowlbeasts. He built a small grave for them, then turned to it and said:
'Now, both of us are in the same boat.'
The boy took it back to his room, and the tiny nest inside became its new home.
The boy would come check on it every day. He liked to gently wipe its plumage while chatting with it, unconcerned with whether it could understand him.
......
Like that one night, when the boy approached it with a sullen face and said:
'I'm confident I have what it takes to be a strong clan leader or a good brother, but I cannot guarantee I can do both at once.'
The boy sighed as he spoke. He contemplated for a long time, before finally running off to return with a box that smelled nice. Inside was his sister's favorite dish.
......
Like that one afternoon, when the boy approached it with a tinge of melancholy in his voice:
'I want to graciously wish Gnosis success on his new journey, yet I selfishly hope for him to stay.'
Perhaps because he had been bottling it in for so long, the boy spent the next half hour explaining to it the situation of the Edelweiss clan, the difficulties facing Gnosis, and his reluctance to part ways with his best friend. In the end, he sighed again and said, 'Alas, you're the only who can hear me out. I'd better think of a farewell gift for him now.'
......
And like that day when its wounds healed, and the boy took it out to the snowy plains to practice flying. When it was about to take off, he took out a black silk scarf, tied the fabric around its neck, and asked:
'Will you come with me?'
—At that moment, the boy had already decided to set aside the burdens of being a clan leader and depart from the Snow Realm to study abroad.
It simply cocked its head and looked at him.
Of course, it did not know what the boy was worried about, why he was anxious, or why he was sad.
But perhaps, it sensed that the boy, just like it, did not wish to stay confined in a warm room. He wished to soar beneath the blue sky—
It spread its wings and leapt forward.
Then, to the boy's happy, surprised shouts, it took off with the wind.
On that day, it learned to fly once again.
uniequip_002_thorns:
Once upon a time, salt was not of this land, just as sand was not of the sea.
Back then, fanatical laws had not yet gripped the land, and a king still sat atop Iberia's royal throne.
Back then, the king was the master of his domain, the mighty forces at his disposal conquering city-state after city-state.
His bravery and renown outlived Catastrophe after Catastrophe, and his forts and outposts sprouted across increasingly remote frontiers.
He erected palaces and great courts, and his cities were filled with statues bearing his image.
But the king could never be sated, for he wished his name to be sung everywhere.
And so, the King of Iberia decreed thusly to his hundred cities:
'Gather all learned men to my royal city, so that I may know of the vastness of the land and sea.'
The first to seek an audience was a merchant, old and frail, yet bearing a treasure he wished to present.
The king trusted in the wisdom afforded by time, and summoned the merchant to his hall.
The merchant presented a burning-hot hourglass, proclaiming that the hottest desert marked the ends of the earth.
'I have once reached the ends of the earth, where the wind scalds like flame and the sun blazes like a torch, and I bring to you the sand of that place!'
The second to seek an audience was a fisherman, youthful and naive, yet bearing a treasure he wished to present.
The king trusted in the wisdom innate to youth, and summoned the fisherman to his hall.
The fisherman presented a flask of black seawater, claiming that the darkest water filled the ends of the sea.
'I have once reached the ends of the sea, where the water is bottomless and the currents run relentless. I bring to you the brine of that place!'
The next to seek an audience was an alchemist, shrouded from sight and of age unknown, yet bearing a treasure he wished to present.
But before the king could decide whether or not to trust this figure, the alchemist appeared within his hall.
He asked the king to give him the hourglass and the flask, and the king readily agreed, curious as to what he would do.
The sand from the ends of the land melted into red liquid before his eyes.
The brine from the ends of the sea crystallized into white sand before his eyes.
The alchemist scattered them both nonchalantly, and they seemed to dissipate into thin air. As if responding to his will, a strong wind blew through the kingdom for three days and nights.
'I know not how vast the land or the sea are, but regardless, neither are as vast as Iberia's boundless power.'
'From now on, the winds of the land and sea obey your will, O King of Iberia.
'Starting today, see to it that a fleet is built, and follow the direction of the wind.'
'Be it by land or sea, Iberia's fleet shall show the way.'
uniequip_003_thorns:
'I lost.' The swordsman puts away his blade, and lowers his head towards the man near the cliff edge.
'You're good.' The other man also puts his sword away, and nods to the swordsman in approval, 'You almost forced me to use that technique.'
'Technique? Which one?' The swordsman grows curious, and instead of waving goodbye, crosses his arms.
The man shows no emotion, but his words stun: 'A move I save for the last moment between life and death. Over the years, everyone who has seen it has either begged for mercy or simply run away... No one has lasted more than three moves.'
'That powerful, huh? Which school did you learn it from?' The swordman's eyes widen.
'Nowhere, I learned it when I was still with my teacher.'
'And who is this teacher of yours...?'
'...No one important. Just an ordinary cleric.'
'An ordinary cleric? Impossible. Your swordplay reminds me of an old friend. Aulus, he was called. He defeated me decades ago.' The swordsman laments, 'If he was your teacher, then I would understand.'
'...No, not him.'
'Alright. You did display a diverse array of swordplay. I'm sure you must have had multiple teachers.'
'...The one who taught me this didn't know swordplay at all. But even he would emerge the victor when my teacher confronted him.' The man shakes his head as he falls into memories of the past.
'Even he would lose to this man...? That's impossible! Who could it be?!' The swordsman's tone turns eager.
'He was hired by my teacher to take care of the students. He seemed a little gloomy and didn't like to socialize with others, so everyone was afraid of him. Start up any trouble, and he'd brandish the mop in his hand and give the offender a good beating.' Recalling his fierce appearance, the man trembles slightly.
'Just a mop? That's nothing to be afraid of.'
'No, the mop always had an unpleasant smell of disinfectant on it. Even the droplets splashing from the head were corrosive.' The man shows a strange expression of admiration of his face. 'I was inspired by him, and installed a tube connected to my longsword, linking to a disinfectant with an improved formula. It is far more corrosive and smells even worse.'
'Now you've gotten me curious. How bad can it get?'
'Are you sure you want a sniff?'
'...Yes, I do.'
The man sighs, unplugs the tube from his blade and approaches the swordsman.
The swordsman takes a deep breath, then his face quickly flashes from white, to red, and then to purple, before finally he drops to the ground.
The man swiftly plugs the tube back to his sword and crouches next to the swordsman. He sees a pair of eyes rolled backward, the swordsman unconscious. After a momentary silence, he finally utters a sentence—
'Phew... I've been holding my breath for so long... but I can still smell it...'
uniequip_002_qiubai:
The bandit recognizes Qiubai.
It was during a summer five or six years ago, when he saw a dying girl lying on the ground in the barrens. The clothes she wore did not appear local, resembling the style of Jiangqi more. 'That's thousands of li away; how did she end up here?' He looked around and found she had nothing with her—no money, no food, no water—yet despite so many people passing by, nobody was willing to help her.
Any other time, and he would've walked away like all the others. But business had been flourishing, and he was in a good mood. Watching the poor girl before him, he couldn't help but think of his own miserable days, when he wished someone would help him... To save someone is an act of great kindness, and today he was more than glad to be a good person and help this girl.
He untied the waterskin from his waist, gave her a few sips, and dragged her into the shade of a boulder. After a while, she opened her eyes. He cracked a satisfied grin, patted her on the shoulder, and left her a few coins. 'Don't cry, girl. Live on.'

Qiubai recognizes the bandit.
It is winter now. Several corpses lie in the sand, covered by a thin layer of powdery snow.
Recently, bandits have been quite active outside the village, and the villagers pooled together their money to hire her to take care of them. They said that after a string of Catastrophes, the harvests in the area were disappointing. With poor harvests came poor business. With no money in their purses, bandits began to sprout up like weeds.
After all the whining and complaining, they began to praise Qiubai's skills. The bandits knew they were at the end of their rope, so they took the village's children hostage. Yet she seized the opportunity and struck, slaying them all in a single strike.
She does not say a thing.
She recognizes the waterskin—or rather, the wine pouch, from which a murky and choking liquor flows—dangling from the waist of a corpse.
She thinks back to the man's smile just a few years ago, and to the few sips of water and coins that had kept her going until she could reach the next town. The corpse still holds in his hand a knife—modified from a farming sickle—blackened by layers of blood both new and old. As for her own blade, it had yet to be wiped clean, and still drips red with fresh blood.
She sets down her bamboo snow hat in front of the waterskin, and folds into it a plum blossom.
uniequip_002_oblvns:
The studio is Sakiko's favorite place in all of Rhodes Island.
Not because it is full of instruments, nor because music lovers gather there.
What Sakiko enjoys is entering the studio while others aren't around, to play the piano by herself.
She plays to practice, to improve, to win, but also to relax.
Whenever something weighs on her mind, there she'd show up, placing the doll from Iris next to her, unraveling her tangled feelings through music. Such are her rare moments of solace.
One such day, Sakiko discovers a note left on the piano.
'Sakiko, thank you for such beautiful piano playing.'
Plain, unbeguiling handwriting. Someone young and easygoing, perhaps.
The notes continued, appearing from time to time.
It seems their writer is quite the shy type.
No name left on them, and the writer is never to be seen in person either. Unwilling to interrupt these precious me time of Sakiko, perhaps.
Whoever they are, they communicate their thoughts to Sakiko day after day.
Whoever they are, they praise Sakiko in every regard. Even for how cute her doll is. For the composure she carries herself with.
Whoever they are, they praise Sakiko's piano playing. Her loss, her strength.
Whoever they are, they thank Sakiko for weaving such sound. In their times of weakness, Sakiko's piano has become something they may lean on.
Whoever they are, they hope to perform with Sakiko.
Whoever they are, they encourage Sakiko. For they can hear Sakiko's loneliness. They support Sakiko with all their heart, even though they know nothing about her problems.
An old friend comes to Sakiko's mind. Perhaps this mysterious one is just like that friend, always struggling to put her feelings into words.
If Sakiko simply looks into the studio's usage records, or shifts her practice times, she'd learn who this mystery correspondent is in no time.
But Sakiko does not do that.
Before we leave Rhodes Island, I want to perform with them.
Just what kind of person could they be? Sensitive? Considerate? Quiet? Timid?
Would they be like Mutsumi? Or Uika?
Whatever the case, they must definitely be a violin player—Sakiko's hunch told her that much, at least.
uniequip_002_hodrer:
By the time class let out, the sun is already setting. Hoederer looks out the window at the deep orange sun, hanging low on the city's edge. Its gentle light filters through gaps in the clouds, illuminating the Babel flag fluttering, mirroring the flag of the Military Commission opposite it. He feels a rare stir of emotion—Kazdel, his broken yet vibrant hometown, was about to settle peacefully into slumber. This was a scene he had only imagined as a child; he couldn't even remember how many times he'd dreamed of it coming true—hundreds? Maybe more?
In the empty room, a knock at the door interrupts his thoughts. He opens it to see a stranger.
'Mr. Hoederer, General Manfred has invited you to pay him a visit,' the stranger says.
'I haven't touched base with the Military Commission in a long time.'
'The General understands. He said you might need some time,' the visitor continues. 'I'm only here as his messenger.'
Manfred... the current head of the Military Commission, who had played a role in Kazdel's development...
'The General also said that if you refused, he'd come see you himself next time,' the messenger adds, before Hoederer can respond.
Manfred, he thinks, lowering his head. The streetlights are starting to come on, and he sees both the messenger and his own shadow begin to blur.
'Please, go back,' he says to the visitor. 'We'll find time to visit the General, but not today.' Then he closes the door.
Hoederer turns around and speaks to the shadows in the empty classroom. 'Welcome back.'
'Hmph.' A figure emerges from the shadows, her back turned to Hoederer. She starts to clean the classroom.
'You hesitated.' Ines remarks.
'I... some things are complicated.'
'Including your feelings on them.'
'Right.'
'You're not denying it.'
'Right.'
'...'
'I told you, our top priority right now is saving enough money to open up that shop you always wanted,' Hoederer says. 'The rest can wait.'
'I know,' she says, pausing slightly. 'I've always known.'
Then they leave together in silence, walking down the street. They look up at the twin gray-blue moons lighting the sky, casting a glow over Kazdel's old district, where ruined buildings stand resilient in the night. Rows of rusted, iron-roofed houses stretch endlessly, and red-brown fields reflect the flickering light from blazing furnaces. Crumbling roads twist through the hills and valleys, carrying the city's lifeblood—an unceasing flow of people—to their destinations.
uniequip_003_hodrer:
Night falls as Hoederer tidies up the last of the goods. He gently lowers the curtain and sits down at the table.
Sheets of paper are scattered all over the table, a dense collection of his observations and experiences over the years. He picks up his pen—the editor wanted these manuscripts by next month, and he needs to finalize his revisions before then.
Hoederer pulls over a sheet with crooked handwriting on it. His fingers trace over the text, and he recalls the rainy night in-between those lines.
Under a rundown roof, he sat next to an old man dressed in rags recounting a decades-long tale. But just as the heart-wrenching climax approached, his pen ran out of ink. He could only pick up a piece of charcoal extinguished earlier from the rain and continue to write—
Suddenly, Hoederer stops his pen. He tries to make sense of the paper's contents, but fails to discern anything from the large water stain and smudged ink.
He puts down his pen and tries to calm himself down. He knows this has happened before—many, many times. Over the years, he's always placated himself with the fact there is no way he can possibly record everything in the land, and mistakes are merely an inevitable part of the process.
But still, he cannot stop thinking about the old man, as if he might suddenly recall every word spoken that night—
Ding-a-ling. The bell on the curtain suddenly chimes, and a child with a small booklet walks up to Hoederer.
'Mr. Hoederer, are you asleep yet?' The child's voice is soft, but her eyes are incomparably bright. 'I finished the essay early, so could you take a look at it?'
Hoederer nods and takes her work.
It is a short diary entry, recounting going out with her family to buy supplies in the shopping district. At the end is an impromptu addendum noting how the current 'shopping street' is different than the former 'aid station'.
'So you recorded... your day out?'
'Yeah! Everyone agreed to write the same topic for the assignment, then we'll see which one you like best! Alder's is about learning how to knit, and Sascha's is about working to help her family... but I still think mine's the most interesting!'
As she talks to her teacher, the girl notices the piles of manuscripts on the table.
'Is this your diary, sir?' the girl asks, tiptoeing. 'It's so much, you must've been writing for years!'
'Yes... twenty years, in fact.'
'Wow, that's amazing!' the surprised girl exclaims as she counts on her fingers. 'We have forty-two kids in our class, so it'd take about a year to write this much?'
'Six months...' Hoederer replies with a smile, but suddenly he feels as if something is lodged in his throat.
He looks again at the pile of papers, all full of various handwritings. For two decades, he has been urging himself to record as much as he can, although always realizing this goal seemed to be beyond reach.
But now, as he looks at the diary entry in his hand, he feels a sort of excitement. He looks forward to tomorrow, when the sun has risen, when the school bell rings, when he will enter the classroom to find forty-two short essays stacked on his desk and waiting for him to read.
uniequip_002_ulpia:
'Laurentina, your outfit looks lovely today,' Blandus's voice comes through the glass of the partition. Laurentina turns with a smile and offers a quick 'thank you' as she gracefully leaves the lab. On the other side, Secunda suddenly stands up from behind the file shelf, staring intently at Ulpianus's back.
After a moment's hesitation, she speaks resolutely. 'Professor, I have a personal question.'
'Ask.' Ulpianus doesn't turn around.
'Why do you always wear the same clothes? You've been dressed like that since the day I met you.'
'Frankly, he's been dressing like that since he was a student. He's hardly changed his outfits at all over the years as I remember, and they always follow the same style, each more buttoned-up than the last. But I'd rather discourage such idle curiosity,' Blandus chimes in.
'Wrong question.' Ulpianus still doesn't turn around, his voice cold and firm.
'Understood!' Secunda answers brightly as she quickly leaves the lab.
Twenty minutes later, she reappears at the door.
'Professor, let me rephrase my question. Why do you rotate between dozens of outfits that look identical but differ slightly in material, craftsmanship, weight, and texture?'
'Still imprecise,' Ulpianus says, casting a quick glance at her before returning to his work sorting the mountain of Seaborn specimens.
Another twenty minutes pass, and Secunda appears again at the lab entrance, pen in hand.
'Professor, I've compared the differences in your outfits and analyzed the changes in your physical metrics, and I've found a preliminary correlation. Considering that combat gear aids Hunters in coordinating bodily movements, I hypothesize that you adjust details in your attire to match changes in your physical state, ensuring optimal control over your body in all conditions.'
After a brief silence, Ulpianus's ear moves slightly, as if signaling her to continue.
'However, this hypothesis leaves some gaps. Is there another variable influencing your choice of attire?'
'Indeed, Secunda.' Ulpianus finally turns around. 'You haven't noticed the correlation between the songs I compose pre-battle and my chosen outfit, but as those compositions have never been recorded, it's understandable you didn't realize this.'
'You mean, the other variable is...'
'My thoughts at the time.'
'Hold on!' At some point, Blandus had emerged from the partition. 'Ulpianus, that's not what you said when you explained it to me! You said it was because you didn't want to attract—'
'There are always more than one reason, Blandus.' Ulpianus cuts him off. 'What I told you was what you needed to know, and what I told her was what she needed to know. Nothing more.'
uniequip_002_pepe:
Pepe folds her arms. The bottom of the heavy curtains shifts ever so slightly before settling back down again.
'Found you. You lose.'
With a sigh, she lifts up the curtains. A cloudbeast pokes its head out from the swathes of fabric, then jumps down onto her foot before scampering off.
'That wasn't me. You lose.'
The voice comes from the cabinet in the corner. It opens, and a boy walks out.
'You shouldn't hide in Mother's room. If Father finds out, he'll get mad.'
'No he won't. He'll just look at me, sigh, and say nothing. Not to mention that he sneaks in himself sometimes.'
'I guess we really are family... Alright, you win. What do you want?'
The boy thinks in silence, fiddling with his fingers, before giving his reply—
'You have Mother's perfume, right?'
'Don't even think about it. She left it to me.'
'There are two bottles, at least give me one of them.'
'It's a set, I can't just split them up.'
'...Fine. She never carried me, so I have no idea what she smells like... I was just curious is all.'
Upon seeing the face so very much like her mother's frown in melancholy, Pepe sinks into a silent reminiscence of her own.
She didn't want to tell her brother that, after so many years, the perfume had long since evaporated, leaving two empty bottles in her drawer.
She also did not want to tell him that she, too, does not remember what their mother smelled like. Time has seen the scent evaporate from her memories as well.
If there was one thing that could remind her of those wondrous bygone days, it was the face she sees in front of her.
'Mother... did give me a pair of storm glasses too. I can give you one, if you'd like?'
'Hmm... But if the weather changes, the maid can tell me.'
'Way to read the room. If you don't want it, fine, have it your way.'
The boy pouts, but just as Pepe thinks he's about to grumble, he breaks out into a gleaming smile, stepping forward to give her a big kiss on the cheek.
'You're the best, Sis.'
Rain begins to pour down outside the window as the solution within the bottle clouds up and tiny star-like crystals form.
Pepe folds her arms as a maid stands quietly by her side and a cloudbeast rubs itself against her feet.
'He didn't take this storm glass with him?'
For a moment, the maid is silent.
'Young Master Senid believes... this storm glass and yours are a pair, and should not be separated.'
Pepe sighs before turning to the maid.
'Then what did he take?'
'Some clothes, a few books, a few pens, and...
'And a portrait of you.'
uniequip_003_pepe:
In light of special permissions granted,
the Field Operations Department has hence passed the following resolution with respect to Pepe:
Where the entailing mission would fall under Reclamation Algorithm scope, this operator shall be pursuant to tactics of a reinforced nature in meeting the enemy.
In witness whereof,
This badge is hereby conferred upon the above named.
'The ancient texts teach that whoever defiles history shall be cursed for all eternity.'
uniequip_002_headb2:
...It's getting dark. We have to leave.
But before we go, take a look at the white vapor of our breath. That's proof that we're alive. And take a look at our friends, buried beneath the damp dirt.
The air is filled with the smell of iron and saltpeter. This is no lecture hall in Grypherburg. Look to your left, at the empty spot where Pencil Stub once sat. He always carried his pen and paper, mulling over the flowery prose of his dramatic scripts. But he was the first to answer my call to raise his fist and resist.
Nika and Yeremey used to sit side-by-side in that empty spot in the middle. I can still see Nika patting Yeremey's back, blushing slightly, singing their school song out of tune after they'd had a few drinks.
And Faddey, too. Whatever his mistakes, he never forgot his duty, and in his last moments, he gave the chance to live to another.
......
There are so many more names. I could go on and on, until we've etched every one of them into our hearts.
Our sorrow is not weakness. It is not cowardice. It is a scar that marks our struggle, and our rebirth, over these ten days. It tells us that there's something that can never be taken away.
We will remember that we each held someone else's hand in ours on that cold winter day, in that all-consuming inferno.
The clouds of dust, the songs that never end, the tears in the snow, the battlefield on which we fought... As long as any of us still remembers—
They will continue to live. We will continue to live.
Ursus cannot kill us, just as life can persist and grow beneath even the frozen earth.
We must remember their faces, remember their fights, and remember that we will meet again, in the future that they died for.
Come and speak their names with me, for those who fell and for those who live, for yesterday and for tomorrow.

Some time later, Sonya found a few battered school uniforms as she was organizing her things. They were wrapped up tightly, not a speck of dust on them.
She touched her burning cheeks, her fingertips numb and trembling as she recalled her speech before the graves in Katorga that day, the words rushing back like snow upon the window.
'What are you doing here, General Zima? Everyone's waiting for you.'
'Don't rush her, Leto. Sonya needs to prepare for the victory banquet.'
They will meet again, in a better place... It wasn't perfect, but they achieved a lot, didn't they?
Sonya gave a subtle smile, and complained to the others about the Ursine winter as she rubbed her hands together.
uniequip_002_chen:
7th of July, clear. On her birthday, she was excited to show Wei Yenwu the unsheathing, but couldn't find a trace of him anywhere. After three days, she waited no longer.
13th of May, cloudy. She cut down a thirty-year-old tree in the courtyard with Tearrender, smashing the roof in. Wei Yenwu did not appear, and merely sent someone to plant a new tree. She never hoped for Wei Yenwu's acknowledgement again.
1st of January, heavy rain. On a New Year's visit, in the downpour, she saw an injustice on her way to the slums, struck out in anger, and took fifteen on her own. In this moment of mortality, she fled into the night by her hilted sword, harming seven, repulsing eight. When she landed atop, Wei Yenwu made a rare appearance, saw the sword marks, and gave her a single look before leaving. She's forgotten why she struck out at the time, but will never forget the disappointment in that look.
25th of December, clear. Acted in bravery while heading home from the Royal Guard Academy, totally fearless, slashing grand and bold, sparing as called for. She was high on spirit, believed she could hew away all injustice in the land.
30th of July, cloudy. At the cost of five days unconscious, let out Shadowless, ultimately cutting down a major fugitive. Lungmen's Ch'en Hui-chieh, shining in prominence. After waking up, Chi Xiao was placed by her bedside, and Wei Yenwu hadn't once come to visit her.
13th of August, overcast. Midway pursuing an Infected criminal, was eager to strike out with Chi Xiao. Chi Xiao did not budge one hair. Subsequently, in this moment of mortality, inspiration struck, Chi Xiao was unsheathed, and cut half a subterranean garage down. She sought Wei Yenwu to find out why Chi Xiao had and hadn't, but Wei Yenwu did not meet her.
30th of September, clear. Chi Xiao was unsheathed a second time, cut open a treasury door, and saved the hostages within. She began to understand, Chi Xiao was a sword of will. She thought she had always done more than enough, but had in actuality done too little. She had to be faster, and mightier.
7th of July, cloudy. On her birthday, over a decade coming, Wei Yenwu asked for the first time to see her swordplay. She condensed all she'd learned, and made an incomplete Cloudsplitter her final examination's answer. Wei Yenwu did not comment.
1st of January, clear. Left Lungmen together with Rhodes Island. From here on forth, Chi Xiao will rarely be unsheathed.
uniequip_003_chen:
The scars on the earth came blitzing in from the horizon, striking true at the Victorian-style complex. The buildings are like a forest torn apart by a whirlwind, collapsed in a radius surrounding a singular point. In these ruins of the Empire, two figures turn over a toppled stele, attempting to find higher ground.
'How long has this place been empty?' Ch'en stands atop the rubble and looks into the distance. The names on the stele behind her once stood for glory, now all but worn away.
Bagpipe's voice comes from somewhere below. 'This school buildin's been abandoned since the war broke out. All the students who didn't complete their course yet got sent off to new campuses, finished the rest out there... Chenchen, that's our old trainin' grounds up in front. You remember?'
'Especially well. I feel like my time as a student was defined by missing out on things. The moment I graduated, they finished repairing the roads, and the training grounds.'
The training grounds have been blown by the shockwave into a plate of jagged protrusions. Ch'en picks up a stone, flings it into a shrub sticking out of a crack in the plate, and a fowlbeast hiding within flies off for somewhere far away, screeching and cawing all the while.
'Things were good enough as is, back then.' Bagpipe's voice comes in close as she stops and stands by Ch'en's ear.
'True. It was probably the simplest time of my life. I didn't have all these issues weighing on my mind, I just had to focus purely on training and studying.'
'That's what drove you? You trained like a maniac every day, got As on every standard subject and all.' Bagpipe clasps her hands on Ch'en's shoulders, and gently rocks back and forth.
'After I returned, I realized just how many things couldn't be solved with swords. There were times I felt far too insignificant, and that even though I worked hard, I couldn't change all that much—sometimes, taking out the enemy doesn't do a thing to address the problem.' Ch'en shakes her head, as if trying to throw her tangled mess of feelings about the past straight out of her brain.
The two of them head up a steep slope. The flowerbed is still where they remember it.
Half of the logo of the once-eminent Royal Guard Academy is submerged in the mud, the other half resting against a fractured stone pillar. Sunset spills across, the light pouring over the symbol now mottled with rust, and what remaining metallic shine there is speaks to the place's former glory.
'It's all changed. Victoria's changed too, hasn't it?' Ch'en mumbles to herself, staring at the crest.
'Some people haven't changed. I went to go visit Instructor Tyrell a few days ago 'cause I knew you were comin'. You were gone in such a hurry back then, you just left all your papers and stuff in the dorms—she's been keepin' them safe all these years. All this is proof of you passin' your studies. Oh, aye, and this too!'
Bagpipe fishes out a stack of documents from her bag, as well as a wooden sword.
'Here's the trainin' sword you used back then. Was meant to go back, technically speakin', but you did so smashin' the instructors were goin' to give you it, y'know, as a surprise for you...'
'Give her my thanks. I left too quickly...'
'At least you've come back now. So many of our year never have, even after all this time.'
The two fall silent.
'Where do you think you'll be in ten years?'
'Who knows? We should be heading back soon. There's still a lot to do.' Ch'en gazes into the distance, off in the direction of Lungmen. 'They arranged everything for me, whether it was going to this school or leaving it. Now, I'm going to go back by myself.'
uniequip_003_irene:
The stranger from the south places her hand on her belt.
The bounty hunters lying at the edge of the cliff watch as she draws two metal tubes, loading them into the 'chamber' of her handcannon.
The startled herd continues to stampede, kicking up clouds of dust as they surge toward the valley below. It would take no more than thirty seconds, the bounty hunters thought, before this southern foreigner with her ocean-borne scent would be trampled into a pulp! Ha! Whether she was holding a firearm or a staff hardly mattered now. Unless she could summon a mountain—
Flames. A thunderous roar.
A natural stone arch between the cliffs is blast open, collapsing before their eyes as rocks tumble down to form a barricade. The frenzied herd yields to this greater force of nature, turns away, and leaves the canyon.
The stranger keeps her handcannon raised, her gaze shifted towards the hunters above.
'Wait... we're not bandits. We can talk this out! Who are you?'
'A Messenger of the Iberian Inquisition.' A flying wasteland fowlbeast casts a shadow briefly over her.
The petite Liberi Messenger places her hand on her belt.
She draws a slender glass vial from her leather buckle, the silver liquid inside reflecting the same stormy light as her pupils. The relentless rain reminds her of storm surges crashing against the coastline, of wounded burdenbeasts abandoned by fleeing people, their screams only heard in the gaps between the thunderclaps.
A Catastrophe Messenger who had turned to the Church. A few families missing in the storm. She knew that the responsibilities Iberia had entrusted to her would not vanish, even as she stepped down from her role as Inquisitor.
She stops, lifting her head, letting the liquid slowly cover her eyes. On that not-so-distant night, when she witnessed the glistening sea crashing against the fortress, her mentor had handed her this potion.
This way, the Flames of Castigation would not sear her eyes, not until Iberia's enemies were burned to the ground.
By morning, she emerges from the woods, her wounds covered in ash. The children behind her hold their hands, blinking their reddened eyes.
'Who are you? Where are the others who went missing?' the people ask, a mixture of gratitude and fear in their voices.
'Irene, Messenger of the Iberian Inquisition,' she replies. 'Now, I have some questions of my own.'
Irene places her hand on her belt.
She pulls a metal canister marked with the Inquisition's seal from a little hook, and soon, reports and letters from Iberia covered your desk at Rhodes Island.
'Irene,' you can't help but ask, 'why is your belt always filled with so many items?'
'These?' She smiles. 'My mentor once told me that in the most critical times, we must carry the 'rations of an Inquisitor.' Look, here's a reload for my handcannon, this is an emergency potion, and here's a canister for sealing letters...'
She spreads her arms, turning slightly.
'People only remember the Inquisitor's lantern and sword, but these, these are what sustain us—the 'rations' we rely on. Everything Iberia has is precious beyond measure. They are part of my responsibilities, and I shall never abandon them.
uniequip_002_irene:
'The miracle child whose life was saved by the Scriptures'—so they all called her at first.
A sudden calamity destroyed the whole town, leaving only her surviving, saved by a passing High Inquisitor and taken back to the Inquisition.
It is typically the Penal Battalion elite that are qualified to become Inquisitors, but she was firm of faith, and it was necessary to her she become one.
She had to commit all the Laws to memory, for she had been chosen.
She had to be first in all classes, for she was special among the special.
In a sparring drill, she was beaten to within an inch by an opponent over ten years her senior, but in spite of it, she refused to fall.
As her awareness neared incoherence, she heard her Maestro tell her one thing.
The Scriptures save people. They did not save you alone.
As if she had heard her Maestro pass judgment on her, she let out a great breath, and for the first time conceded her loss.

'High Inquisitor Dario's darling disciple'—as many people came to speak of her later on.
If the proper verdict is not written in the Scriptures, then it must come from her Maestro's mouth.
She was so firm of faith, yet could never pass evaluation.
Until one time, she involuntarily blurted out a judicial opinion contrary to her Maestro.
Her Maestro repealed her verdict, but gave her a nod to see.

'Inquisitor Irene'—so she frequently proclaimed herself, from the day she was formally appointed by the Inquisition.
Her Maestro spoke that she had to make her own judgments.
She turned through the past archives again and again, sped to scenes of greatest danger one after another, and within a few brief years, she had resolved close to a hundred cases.
Each time she reported her verdicts to her Maestro, he would refuse to comment.
Until they bade farewell on the shore of Gran Faro, and she confronted the ocean alone and the menace it delivered.
The Scriptures, the Maestro, and the Self.
All wills merged as one in the face of true danger, becoming the fire that blazes forth from her handcannon.

'Irene, Inquisition Messenger of Iberia.'
So the dainty Liberi introduced herself aboard Rhodes Island.
She still proudly lifts her head. The look in her eyes is more resolute than it ever was before, undying as the reefs of Iberia's coastline that will never see themselves drowned again.
uniequip_004_irene:
In light of permissions granted sui gratis, the Field Operations Department has hence passed the following resolution with respect to Irene:
Where the entailing mission would fall under Integrated Strategies scope, this operator shall be pursuant to tactics of a reinforced nature in meeting the enemy.
In witness whereof,
This badge is hereby conferred upon the above named.
'You shall go through the harshest of trials.'
uniequip_002_blkkgt:
Among Degenbrecher's luggage is a case exclusively for storing her medals. After making exceedingly short work of her operator exam, the remaining downtime was spent with her enlightening our HR operators as to their significance.
- Knight-Champion of Kazimierz Medal
Black medal of crossed swordbreakers, lying unassumingly in center of case. Design makes it immediately clear that Kazimierz tailored this champion's medal to her. She reigned for three straight years and so was given three, but only the first was personally awarded to her by the Grand Knight after usurping the defender. Which is why she didn't throw it away, and why it's the one artifact of Kazimierz she still carries with her.
'Commemorative enough, barely.'
- 'Thanks'
Inverted triangle inscribed with Kjerag's holy Mount Karlan. Not issued by any official organization, rather forged for her by clan head Ratatos at the request of a household under Browntail rule. Degenbrecher had rescued said household's members from an avalanche.
'This first one was almost ten years ago now. I know they meant it nicely, and I don't mind how it looks. But the news spread, and now I get one of these medals from the Tri-Clans any time I do something similar. The cupboard at home is full of them.'
- 'The Silverashes' Sword and Shield'
Second medal from the left, sword and shield motif. All of Karlan Trade knows that those wearing this medal are free to act unimpeded wherever Karlan Trade is concerned. Initially a pass designed expressly for her by Enciodes, but as soon became apparent, nobody simply overlooks the presence of Degenbrecher. Its worth these days is instead in gently reminding others that she is affiliated with Karlan Trade.
'One day, I forgot to wear this one. Enciodes went that entire day quieter than usual, then in the end asked if I had any complaints with the company.'
- 'Kjeragandr's Soldier'
Third medal, honorary decoration issued by the Vine-Bead Court, was worn by Enya herself when she formally became the Saintess.
'This was the biggest protest the Saintess could make back then. I don't think much in particular about Kjeragandr—at most, I think I'd like to take Her on.'
- '10 Years'
To mark ten years of acquaintance, Enciodes rustled up a little gift for her, effectively commemorating her Karlan Trade decennial at the same time. It may not have been founded when they first met, but the blueprints were already laid out in his heart.
'I didn't even recall what it was commemorating when he gave me this. A token of thanks, I suppose, but I'm sure he just wanted to let me know that he still remembered the big words he said back when it all began. Speaking of Kjerag... if you're ever there as a tourist and want to find somewhere quiet, you can ask me.'
uniequip_002_huang:
'...Each and every Deputy Minister entered into the Haoran Pavilion has a history with an intractable case, one that tried to elude their very investigation.'
'No wonder you care so much about my deal, ***. It's just complicated enough for you, right? Just listening to that huge string of numbers makes my head want to explode.'
'No. It's because of a predecessor of mine.'
'Care to explain?'
'The year I'd just assumed Deputy Minister duties at the Central Judicial Office, I'd been rummaging through files in light of a case I had, only to find that in order to fell a great villain, he'd employed counterfeit evidence at their impeachment. Despite him already being retired at the time, I convinced the Censor to recall him to the capital for punishment.'
'Uh, I'm not going to weigh in on whether that was right for you to do or not. Can I ask what this has to do with me?'
'I only later came to know that said predecessor had not retired under normal circumstances, and was frankly not in his hometown caring for his family as one would assume... He'd concealed his identity and been appointed to chase down a series of unsolved cases... At the time, he'd practically figured out the third child's whereabouts, and it was exactly then when I just so happened to learn of his early mistake—what are you doing? Stop rubbing my shoulder...'
'You were used. Which also means, if it wasn't for this case, my dad's whole deal would've come to light forever ago, huh?! No need to pull that face, I'm not blaming you for this. All I can say is that this is a real complicated affair... Don't let me interrupt you, go on.'
'At the time, your father had suddenly been given a transfer. He departed for Victoria; in the two weeks following my predecessor being taken into custody, the Central Judicial Office scrollery suffered an inexplicable fire one night, and all the south's documents were reduced to ash... The Tianshi are correct. As a Central Judicial Office Deputy Minister, I must investigate the truth of this matter, and to do so, I must renounce my very Central Judicial Office Deputy Minister status... hence why I must take it on now.'
'You can't give me that again! Tell me everything you know, now. All of it. Chop-chop.'
'No. You can't help me. These days, you are no more than 'a Victorian lodging aboard Rhodes Island.' You need only tell me what you know, all the things you've been through, and you can leave the rest to me.'
'And I call that crap! The guy who died the land's most inexplicable death in a whole other country was my dad, not yours, and the woman who's dead according to her official paperwork and had to spend so long without a life except one on the move is me, not you. You may as well have never taken your mask off here, if it wasn't gonna make you any better at talking to me! Jeez, I know what you're worrying about, but there's nothing to fear! I'm an Elite Operator of Rhodes Island! Have you seen me with my chainsaw or not? Have you experienced my heat or not? I don't CARE how complicated the case is or how many enemies we've got, you think they get to burrow away in the shadows their entire lives?'
'......'
'...Oh, yeah, did you mention just now your predecessor chased down that third kid's whereabouts?'
uniequip_003_huang:
She picks up the logistics operator stunned by the cannon blast and throws them behind her, but does not leave. Looks like she still wants to say something—
Then the whole world goes black.
'She's not in good shape.'
She hears someone talking, not too far away... She tries to open her eyes, but everything seems broken and blurred, like a heavily damaged video tape.
She sees two people sitting opposite each other, one wearing a familiar mask, the other lost in thought, gazing down at her stethoscope.
They argued for a long time about what to do with her. In the end, neither seems happy with the conclusion. Finally, the one with the stethoscope comes over to her, writing down the monitor readings as she says,
'You can stay here. You'll have a new name.'
She recognizes Kal'tsit, but is unsure if she has ever seen Dr. Kal'tsit looking so worried.
'Maybe it's a glitch in my memory.' She says to herself—
An ear-piercing buzzing interrupts her thoughts.
Warm, yellow light fills her vision. She is standing in front of the door to her house. The tiles beneath her feet are softer than marshmallows.
Her mother is writing a letter. There is a box full of them by her mother's feet. Unsent letters have long since taken the place of tears.
She tries to comfort her mother, tell her she is alright, but her mother does not seem to see her.
She wants to take a closer look at the letter, but all she sees are countless scribbles like an indecipherable puzzle.
She tries to rearrange the scribbles into something comprehensible, but they suddenly fade and disappear.
No—she anxiously grasps at the last scribbles—where? She cannot see her hands—she wants to see—
She sees her own silhouette outside the window. She remembers now. This was the day when she left home.
The house collapses into a wound before her eyes. She tries to press at the wound, to stop the blood from gushing out...
Someone grabs her shoulder—'Stop. This one's gone.'
But she continues to press, until black rocks grow from the wound, pierce her hands, and start to grow from her body too.
She does not care. She clenches her teeth and keeps pressing, until the wounded starts coughing and says—
'The textile workers of Connor County will remember everything you did for home. Never bow to those criminals.'
Home? Was Connor County really her home? She gazes at the worker leader, whose neck was cleaved by an attacker, but sees only the logistics operator stunned by the shell—
'Emergency defibrillation—done! Check the pupils!' The operator shouts before he is pushed away by Blaze.
'You're awake! Another shell got you—whoa!' Blaze grabs his head and pushes him back inside the shelter, then picks up her chainsaw from the ground.
'What are you doing?' The operator asks in a worried tone.
Blaze spits out the clotted blood in her mouth.
'Getting back into the fight.'
uniequip_002_gvial2:
Torches crackle softly in the low wooden hut. A gust of wind whistles through the cracks in the boards. A few shadows gently sway.
'Come in.'
The hut door is hefted open, and a mass of somewhat hasty green squeezes into the firelit space, having to get far more intimate with the doorframe than doorframes typically experience.
'Got everything?'
'Y—You bet...' Gavial gives her head an impromptu massage.
'Bring it out.'
Gavial hoists her tail back to bundle up the bag behind her, and takes great care to open it up on the table. Out fall a wide assortment of weapons. Those standing around the table grab one each.
'Dagger.'
'Cutting edge is sharp. Signs of whetstoning.'
Another voice makes itself known. Gavial twists her head around looking for it, only to quickly give up and pull it back.
'Chainsaw.'
'No junk in the chain, lubrication on drive shaft is fresh, and handle wraps have been changed before. Motor system is running well, power system is stable.'
'Uh-huh. The axe?'
'About the same condition as the chainsaw. The only difference is the axe has some slight rusting...'
'Don't mind her. The metal was rusted when I made it.' Yet another voice has emerged.
'...Didn't you tell me you used the best materials?'
'Those are the best materials. Even the 'Rage Ironhide' didn't get it as good as this.'
'Quit it a sec, you two, we're not done yet... Gavial.'
'Here...'
'Where's your staff?'
'Muhh, my staff...' Gavial hangs her head low.
'Where is your staff? Bring it out.'
Gavial realizes she's not winning this, grinds her teeth, and pulls her staff out of her boot. Well, boots.
'Staff's... broken.'
'How did you break it?'
'Clobbering people out there over the last few days. I just gave it a whack once and... it snapped.'
'How? You know I reinforced it. All you had to do was take good care of it and... Gavial, give me the inspection form. Have you filled it in properly?'
'No duh I did!'
'What were you doing last month on the 3rd? You were meant to give it maintenance that day, but you've written nothing here. Did you forget?'
'Did not. I was, uh, I was busy that day with... oh! No, I got it! I was scrapping with the Durins' machines! You even gave them the blueprints for those!'
'I do recall that, but it doesn't change the fact you wrecked your staff, so...'
Gavial sucks in a deep, deep breath. 'So like you laid out. Five days without eating meat. I'm ready for it...'
After a brief silence, with the table shooting a few glances between each other, there's the sudden telltale 'pfft' of a laugh.
'What the hell's so funny... Tomimi? Zumama? Inam! What are you guys laughing for?' Gavial asks through a frown of complete suspicion.
Inam is scratching at her head. 'Gavial, the fact that you can take proper care of your weapons is impressive. I wonder if we can thank the statue being erected...'
'I literally guaranteed you guys! You didn't even believe me?!'
'We're only finding out in the first place because people tell us you keep complaining about weapon upkeep being a hassle,' Zumama explains.
'We wouldn't let you go without meat for five days, Gavial... that would be too scary for you,' Tomimi quietly adds.
Gavial sighs a slow sigh of relief. 'Scared the hell outta me. I seriously thought you guys were gonna have me lashed down...'
'I'll make you another staff. Remember to care for it regularly!'
'Yeah, you don't have to tell me... huh? Something smells good. Is that—'
'That said, seeing how we know you, we decided we'd punish you via other means... This is a whole pot of Acahualla-sourced meat stew!' Inam unveils. 'Gavial, you have to stand over there and watch us while we eat the entire thing.'
Gavial's eyes pop out of her skull. 'You guys are torturers! ACTUAL TORTURERS!'
uniequip_003_gvial2:
Once more, Gavial smashes open the door, grabs Minimalist by the collar, and hauls him to the infirmary.
'I told you, I'll be there as soon as I finish this design!'
'But your blueprints haven't changed a bit since yesterday!'
'I'm just waiting for that lightbulb to go off in my head!'
'That's Avdotya's thing, Stitch, not yours. If you keep delaying the treatment, the only things going into your head will be my fists.'
'Didn't you say you only beat up bad guys?'
Gavial grins smugly. 'I'll make an exception just for you, especially if you keep refusing treatment.'
Minimalist's face flickers between anger and a suspicious grin.
'He's definitely plotting something,' Gavial thinks.
But whatever scheme he comes up with, she couldn't care less.
For the next week, Minimalist stops talking about designs, drawings, or inspiration. Eventually, Gavial makes an inquiry.
'So how's that design you were working on?'
'It's fine.'
'Is it for the entertainment facilities in New Zeruertza?'
'Something like that. Hmph. It's a surprise—ow!'
The needle is removed, the injection is complete.
Gavial is utterly uninterested in whatever 'surprise' Minimalist is cooking up.
Another week passes. A message arrives: Gavial has been chosen as a special guest for the next big celebration in New Zeruertza, and a 'surprise' has been prepared. Inam tells her that if she has time, she should come back, take a look, and do the ribbon-cutting.
'A surprise?' she mutters, puzzled.
Just then, a crowd bursts into the infirmary. Minimalist trails behind with a large box in his arms.
'Inam figured you wouldn't have time in your busy schedule, so we brought you your gift ahead of time,' says Zumama. 'It's a scale model of your new statue.'
'A new statue? Didn't they already build one? And I specifically told them not to give it a thick tail.'
'Well, you'll have to ask Stitch about that. He's the one who designed this latest one.'
An uneasy feeling rises in her.
Stitch steps forward.
'This is for you, Gavial. A token of thanks for all you've done for New Zeruertza.'
He opens the box. Inside is a miniature statue of Gavial, with a thick, oversized tail jutting from the back.
Gavial's face cycles through a wave of different emotions.
'If that's to scale, then won't the tail on the real statue be thicker than her entire body?' Tomimi asks.
'If it's supposed to be proportional, then use my actual proportions!' Gavial growls, teeth clenched. 'This is way thicker than it should be!'
Stitch starts clapping. He can tell that she really does care about his little 'surprise' after all.
Weeks later, Zumama pushes open the door to find Gavial using the little statue to sharpen her chainsaw.
'Sharpening your weapon, Gavial?'
'No, just trying to grind down this statue's stupid tail!'
'Where's Stitch?'
'How should I know? Ugh. Alright. I just think that before I go back for the ribbon-cutting, somebody had better make sure the statue in Acahualla has its tail resized right.'
'Or else what? Is that a threat?'
Gavial lifts her chainsaw, its blade gleaming bright from the polishing.
Gavial decides to let her threat remain a mystery for now.
uniequip_002_surtr:
'Sami blesses and protects us all. It is everywhere, and ever watchful over Its children.
'Every tree, every blade of grass in this tundra is part of It, and through them It guides us. Even in distant lands, It reaches through these mediums to aid us in troubled times.
'So what do you say? A handcrafted Sami spirit stone? Even the great Arges bought one, you know.' —A certain incorrigible Sami peddler
As Surtr, amidst the heart of the blizzard, prepared to leave the icefields' depths, Sami gave her a gift.
Slowly, the sheaves of frozen runes revealed to her melted, crumbled, and a stone of crystal ice fell at her feet.
As if compelled, Surtr picked it up, and found it not nearly as bone-chilling as its looks suggested. Even as the blizzard bathed it, it pulsed with a warmer rhythm. Almost a familiar one. The rhythm of life.
Such a familiar feeling. She looked at the sword in her hand, staring at the molten core within it.
Bringing the crystal to her sword, Surtr could feel... another self stirring, a voice crying out, 'Damn you, take that thing away! Get it out of my sight!'
So, Surtr bought one of those locally handcrafted Sami pendants, discarded its useless rock, and replaced it with the crystal. She wound the rope around the sword's hilt.
With every step forward, the pendant and hilt would knock together in rhythm—clank, clank. This annoyed her other self greatly, haughty yet powerless to resist.
In the back of her mind, Surtr couldn't help but laugh at it.
She knew it was a seething, scorching sort, easy to irritate, hated cold things the way one might hate the sound of nails on a chalkboard.
It was why she'd always loved ice cream, and all cold refreshments alike.
Clank, clank—Surtr knocked the pendant on the blade a few times, and it gave a few violent shakes in response, before settling down once more. The crystal's blue light bathed the blade's flame red, smothering it somewhat.
Thank you, Sami.
She could feel its blaze becoming wrath, increasingly unable to bear being slighted so, as if saying, 'You fool! You would choose this most pathetic, most damnable of means to get back at me!'
Nonsense.
She'd never considered its minor griping a threat, with or without Sami's help.
She's never seen her fiery powers as a blessing, nor has she ever felt restricted by the chaos that is her memory. Headstrong and self-centered, she disregards and cherishes as she sees fit.
Feranmut fragment? Big deal. Just shut it in front of me.
uniequip_003_surtr:
As she visited the new dormitory in Victoria, Surtr knew much had happened to Rhodes Island while she was away.
Her new room was clean and tidy. Just as the message she received on her return journey had said, there were no decorations other than the personal belongings she had kept in her old room. It was so simple it felt almost cold.
Her personal belongings were few: a few health monitoring instruments, some clothing, and everyday items.
But there was also a strange box on a table in the middle of the room, looking decidedly out of place.
She opened the box and read the letter inside. Apparently, it contained gifts that the other operators had left her.

You're going to Sami? Then take this self-heating travel mug. I also included the recipes for a few hot drinks you can make on your own to keep yourself warm out there!
—Hibiscus
'...But I just got back from Sami.'

I heard you can't remember your past either. This is my old recording terminal. Maybe you can use it to keep a log of important memories while you're traveling.
—Rosmontis
'She must have misunderstood my memory disorder. But sure, I could use it to record sights and sounds on my travels.'

Thank you for helping out with the combat simulations. This is a Blacksteel custom-made battery-powered portable ice-maker, so that you can have cold drinks even while you're traveling!
—Jessica
'But it doesn't come with any batteries... Although I suppose this chunk of ice from Sami will fit in it.'

There was also a camping stove from Meteorite, a travel bag from another operator, and various other items she sorted through one by one.
Surtr found herself rather pleased at the sight of a whole table covered with things that seemed useful, but really weren't.
She was never a talkative person, nor particularly eager to help others. She disliked trouble and never used to go out of her way for strangers, not when she had plenty on her plate already.
But now, as part of Rhodes Island, she realized that she had so many people around her who cared about her.
This sort of relationship was unfamiliar, but not unwelcome.
She put her usual terminal, clothes, and other travel items in the storage cabinet, and set aside space in her backpack for the recording terminal she had never used before, the ice-maker she was not sure would work, the unfamiliar camping stove, the self-heating mug... She wanted to bring them with her, rather than leave them in her room.
She picked up the backpack with a frown. It was rather heavy.
But this way, she would certainly remember the ones who gave these to her, no matter where she went.
uniequip_003_vvana:
Many years have passed since the people of Kazimierz decided their nation no longer had need of the night. Now, a giant artificial moon pours light down Kawalerielki, illuminating every nook and cranny as if the sun is out.
An unassuming old lady sits by the window. She has lived a long life, a life so long that every knight of the past has been long buried, and every Kazimierzian has now become a new sort of 'knight'. According to the latest regulations, every citizen should practice this 'grand chivalry' and be productive for at least seventy-two hours before each rest break. It is said that the light left behind by the Radiant Knight who 'brought chivalry back to Kazimierz' will always keep them going—provided they have gone through the photosynthetic module surgery.
At a waste disposal facility bathed in light, a box of candles is crushed flat. No one needs light anymore, no one remembers candles existed, and of course not a soul knows that this city once went crazy for a certain Candle Knight.
Inside the city engulfed with so much light it bleaches and blurs the skyline, the old woman vaguely outlines the course of her life. Because she was the Candle Knight of Kazimierz, several hospitals were built on her recommendation. Because she was an Empresses' Voice of Leithanien, several schools were reorganized as she envisioned. She traded her title as an envoy of peace who extinguished the flames of war with her candlelight for plots of land to rehome refugees, and exchanged her reputation as a hero who cleaved the Kargereich with her blade for monuments to remember the victims lost to disasters. Even her scandals managed to secure a sanatorium for wounded and retired knights.
But today, people have forgotten the Candle Knight, the Empresses' Voice, the envoy, the hero, and even the scandals they once relished in reading. Viviana's own name cannot be traded for anything. With all her identities stripped away, the real Viviana remains trapped in a tiny room, just like little Vivian years and years ago.
Vivian asks her: will the real Viviana never get to leave the little room?
She is silent for a long time before shaking her head. Even so, she says, there are some things only the child trapped inside the room can do.
And what is that, Vivian asks.
Something Viviana already did, she says, even in broad daylight: she would dive beneath the covers, light a candle, and read a knight novel.
So just being unruly... Vivian's head droops down.
But how could she not be at this moment? Like the knight in the tale who unrulily believed his lance could kill the swells as dark as night, she also unrulily believed her tiny candlelight could steal the sun's radiance, if only for a moment.
Viviana twirls the wick of the last candle. A tiny flame casts a tiny shadow.
The aftermath of Arts cast by a dying person does not take long for the General Chamber's emergency response team to handle—but for a few short hours before that happens, Kawalerielki is shrouded in shadow for the first time in a long while, and its people finally got a rare, peaceful moment of rest in the temporary darkness.
—An excerpt from a novel written by an anonymous author, first discovered in front of a blank monument. No one knows if it is fiction or not, but it started a years-long tradition of people lighting candles before the monument.
uniequip_002_vvana:
Multiple people have opined to me at length about what they think of Nova Knightclub's 'plans', how my 'vacation' might signal the Knightclub's future decisions, and so on and so forth. Still, as the Grand Knight Territory and its ghastly white glowing metal walls faded beyond the horizon, all those speculations lost their meaning.
In my mind, I was simply being sent to yet another place not of my choosing. The silver lining, at least, is that I don't hate it here. Every morning in Ognisko, all the workshops fire up their furnaces at almost the same time, and the blacksmiths all hail each other good morning over the clamor of fire and metal. It's an organic, living noise that pays no heed to what outsiders bring or take away.
I took up assistant duties in an arms workshop to stave off the boredom. Orders are always coming in from Kawalerielki, with plenty of familiar names attached. Nova is now raising a 'Moonlight Knight' who uses a sword made of fluid alloy—I only later found out they swapped those red wine baths and handsome manservants for moonlight hammocks and silver-furred manglerbeast sidekicks. In contrast, the blacksmith at my workshop never asks which knight she's forging for, nor does she care who I am—be it the Candle Knight or a commoner—and isn't concerned whether her weapons go to competition knights or barren mercenaries. She never reads the 'knight persona' briefing attached to any of her orders.
But she does care about her craft. Sometimes, I'll stop and admire the fire in the hearth, and she'll proudly recount the tale of how the first fire came from the heavens. It fell to the land in its divinity, and where it fell the land was blessed with metal, and thus the craft of smelting and forging was born. 'Shame,' she said once, 'that nobody believes any of it now.'
I told her that when I was very young, I saw fire falling from the heavens. She listened, and then she laughed, sensing how cursory my words were, how I was trying to save her from embarrassment. Changing the subject, she asked if I'd like to raise the ceiling's workshop a little, so I wouldn't have to walk everywhere stooped over. I declined, and she said no more.
As if by coincidence, on my second day, a radio program came on with an astronomical report, forecasting a meteor over Ognisko. After all the furnaces in town went out that night, the blacksmith and I stood by the workshop door, and saw blue ripples across the sky. According to an old folksong, those are made as the meteors stir the starpod, though this meteor remained hidden behind the hills.
The blacksmith's eyes were all aglow. Her feet set in motion, as if to chase that blazing light.
After running some distance, she turned to look back at me.
'Aren't you coming?'
'I'm fine watching from here. The ripples its tail leaves in the sky are beautiful, too.'
I did lie, in a way, when I told her I'd seen fire falling to the ground as a child. It was true a meteor crossed Sturmland's skies, but only the window on the wrong side was opened in my room. I didn't want to wake Father and beg him to take me outside. I never saw a meteor that evening, and so instead I clutched my ice-cold binoculars and told myself, 'It's fine. The ripples its tail leaves in the sky are beautiful, too.'
And no, I was never in denial about just how achingly stunning the blazing glint of the meteor itself could be. I just never spoke of it. Just as every time I light a candle, I see only the shadow beneath it.
The blacksmith vanished into the night. I looked all around, and saw the burdenbeast tethered by the workshop door. In all the knight novels, Kuranta knights could cross entire prairies on their own two feet, never in need of a steed. But I am no Kuranta, and right now, no knight either—This thought crossed my mind as I mounted the burdenbeast and rode off, chasing where the meteor had vanished.
uniequip_002_siege2:
Vina never expected her meeting with the Doctor after reboarding to take so long.
When she strolled through the Command Center doors on a whim, she never would have guessed the intense discussions the Doctor and Closure were having was about a board game of all things. Londinium's newest fad—The Adventure of the Lioness. There were only so many ways to kill time in the pubs right now, and this game for kids quickly found a home among pubgoers who loved picking at politics.
To all that, the Doctor replied: 'Closure and I see plenty of unpatched holes in the game design.'
She prepared to deploy her standard suite of excuse-mes and beat a hasty retreat, but Closure had already sealed off her escape route, and was urging her to join in. 'I can vouch. This game really takes me back to those days, you know? Underground in Londinium, fighting with the Self-Salvation Corps.'
And how was she to predict that a fun little idea from a couple of kids playing house would get snapped up, commercialized, shipped, and become all the rage in Londinium? And then the greatest surprise was Morgan gleefully bringing the game back to the landship and recommending it to everyone she possibly could.
'I'll play as you.' Taking on the 'Vina' role, the Doctor readied for the other two players' assault. Dice rolled again and again, and each time City Keeper 'Vina' came out on top, even twice succeeding in a complete counteroffensive and taking the 'Caster' territory for 'herself'.
Defeated time and time again by 'herself', Vina was somewhat exasperated. 'Doctor, this is cheating. Hardly anything you're doing is in the rulebook.'
'We never agreed to play by anyone else's rules, Vina.
'Londinium's an enormous city. There are plenty to draw on that the designers didn't know or care about. That's what I meant by holes.'
For a moment, Vina thought to herself, then threw herself decisively into the next round. The aftermath of an independent Tara, the strategic give-and-take of Caster, the Infected vanguard bearing news of Gododdin... Vina played character after character, trying with all her might to wrest the Doctor's advantage away, but always to minimal effect.
Before her eyes was a city that far surpassed her expectations. With a peculiar and twisted ambition, she sought to beat 'herself'.
But it was beyond her to read any of the strange and crafty angles by which the Doctor defused her offensives. Their tiny little board couldn't support the three's game anymore. With a flash of inspiration, Closure called directly on PRTS to simulate one that was even larger and more complex.
'Uh. Closure, are you allowed to use PRTS like that? What if Dr. Kal'tsit—'
Closure waved it off. 'She's got urgent business, she's not on the ship. Besides, I have the permissions to guarantee she'll never find out what we did.'
An absurdly protracted ten hours later, Vina finally had to excuse herself from the game thanks to an anonymous express delivery to her dormitory.
What had arrived was the yet-to-be-published first expansion for the game, including a series of all-new powers with all-new game plays. There was Normandy, Ashworth, and the Unicorn. Printed on the box was a roadmap for future expansions and updates, too.
'The Adeptus Chamber Knights, the Empire's Blades, the Agents of Operation Boulder, the Twins' Voices, and the Angels of Judgement...'
